## The problem

Our twelve-person engineering team has been running on long-lived feature branches for over a year, and the cost is compounding. Branches routinely live two to four weeks before merging, and every extra day widens the gap between branch and mainline. The result is predictable:

- Merge conflicts have become large, multi-file affairs that eat entire afternoons and often require the original author and a reviewer to untangle together.
- Integration bugs surface late, sometimes only in staging, because code from different branches never runs together until the final merge.

We are effectively deferring integration risk to the worst possible moment, right before a release, when we have the least time to absorb surprises.

## The proposal

I propose we move to trunk-based development: everyone commits small, frequent changes directly to main, guarded by feature flags for anything incomplete, and short-lived branches (under a day) only where CI requires it. Concretely:

- Adopt feature flags for any change that can't ship complete in a single day, so main stays releasable at all times.
- Require CI to pass before merge, with a fast pipeline (under ten minutes) so frequent merging doesn't become a bottleneck itself.
- Set a team norm of merging at least once per day per active workstream, reviewed in small increments rather than one large diff.

This shrinks the gap between individual work and the shared codebase, which is precisely what eliminates the conflict and late-integration problems above.

## What could go wrong

The strongest objection is real: small, frequent merges to main increase the risk that half-finished, poorly-flagged work destabilizes production, especially before our discipline around flags and CI matures. A team used to isolating risk in branches may temporarily see more incidents on main, not fewer, during the transition. I take this seriously rather than waving it away — it argues for a deliberate rollout (pilot with one or two workstreams, invest in flag tooling and CI speed first) rather than a flip-the-switch mandate. Done carelessly, this could genuinely be worse than what we have.

I would like a decision by the end of next week.
